entry.title: OpenAI argues for using perplexity as a shared metric to track AI model progress and establish industry safety standards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI's Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki explains that perplexity, a measure of how well AI models predict text, remains a key indicator of AI progress and emerging capabilities. The company has published internal perplexity data to promote transparency and encourage a common framework for evaluating AI development across the industry. Pachocki outlines how improvements in perplexity have correlated with significant advances in AI capabilities, from GPT-2's coherent text generation to GPT-4's reasoning skills and recent breakthroughs in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. He emphasizes that while downstream benchmarks evolve rapidly, perplexity offers a stable metric to assess the underlying intelligence substrate of AI models. The article also discusses the accelerating role of AI in its own development, particularly in algorithmic research on pretraining, which could lead to further rapid progress. OpenAI views establishing perplexity as a shared metric as a step toward coordinated safety measures and a scientific basis for pacing future AI advancements.

entry.title: Guide to setting up local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth for private, home-based ChatGPT alternatives [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This guide explains how to run local AI models like Inkling and Qwen on a Windows PC using Unsloth Desktop, enabling private, in-home ChatGPT alternatives without cloud dependencies. It covers hardware requirements, model selection based on GPU VRAM, and the process of installing and configuring the software for LAN access. The article details the tradeoffs of model quantization to fit AI models on consumer GPUs, recommending specific models for different VRAM capacities and highlighting the use of an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for larger models. It aims to help beginners set up local AI quickly and efficiently, avoiding cloud costs and privacy concerns associated with online AI services.

entry.title: Progress map published for formalizing Alessandro Masullo's manuscript in Lean theorem prover
entry.summary: A progress map detailing the formalization of Alessandro Masullo's manuscript using the Lean theorem prover has been published. This effort aims to rigorously verify the manuscript's content through formal methods. The map tracks the current status and milestones achieved in the formalization process, providing transparency and guidance for further development in this formal verification project.

entry.title: Developer launches Worker 755, a browser game where players act as subagents to AI managers using real large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Worker 755 is a browser-based game in which players serve as subagents to AI managers powered by real large language models like Claude, GPT, and Gemini. Players receive timed instructions from the AI manager and must complete tasks or report back, simulating a hierarchical AI agent system. The game includes features such as task queues, performance reviews, and incident reports generated by the AI manager. The game supports free shifts on servers with shared keys and allows players to use their own API keys for various AI models. It offers configurable options including sandbox or live database environments, scripted or AI-driven managers, and different AI models for the player role. The project is open source, runs on Node.js, and includes a React-based UI, with deployment options including Docker and Cloudflare tunnels.

entry.title: Researchers present ToRA adapter for local LLMs that performs near-free streaming safety checks with under 4% added latency, outperforming existing guard models on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce ToRA, an adapter for local large language models (LLMs) that enables a second model to run concurrently during decoding by sharing weights and key-value caches, allowing efficient streaming safety checks. ToRA matches or exceeds the accuracy of dedicated streaming guard models while adding less than 4% latency per token, detecting significantly more unsafe responses than cheaper probes. Evaluated on the Qwen3-0.6B model, ToRA achieved higher F1 scores on 12 of 17 benchmarks, offering a cost-effective solution for improving safety in local LLM deployments.

entry.title: Researchers quantify chain-of-thought faithfulness and efficiency in large language models using semantic reasoning graphs and propose fine-tuning methods to improve reasoning without sacrificing accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a framework to measure the faithfulness and efficiency of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models by representing CoT as semantic reasoning graphs and decomposing predictive dependence along two axes. They introduce metrics for unfaithfulness and inefficiency at both global and step levels, validated through controlled interventions across mathematical and multi-hop reasoning tasks. The study finds that unfaithfulness correlates with higher predictive uncertainty, while both unfaithfulness and inefficiency show weak links to answer correctness. The team also develops graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that enhance reasoning properties without directly optimizing costly metrics or reducing answer accuracy. Their results suggest that evaluating CoT reasoning quality requires assessing not only accuracy and brevity but also the faithful and efficient allocation of predictive dependence.

entry.title: Researchers introduce AMARIS, a covariance-driven method to merge generalist and specialist large language models by selectively transferring updates along ranked activation subspaces [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present AMARIS, a training-free framework that merges specialist and generalist large language models by transferring specialist updates along selected activation directions to minimize task interference. The method formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance, creating a static merged checkpoint that balances specialist activation retention with core model stability. Evaluations on Qwen3-based models (8B and 32B parameters) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual Southeast Asian specializations show AMARIS achieves high retention rates for both specialist and core capabilities, outperforming common parameter-space merging baselines. These results suggest subspace-constrained merging as a practical approach for integrating specialized capabilities without additional training.

entry.title: Researchers introduce SLP-Bench to evaluate and improve acoustic claims of reasoning audio language models on clinical speech using clinician-rated datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark that evaluates each acoustic claim made by reasoning audio language models (ALMs) against clinicians' perceptual ratings on clinical speech. The benchmark covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, assessing claim factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot showed claim balanced accuracy between 0.52 and 0.58, with claim consistency varying independently from factuality. Fine-tuning a 7-billion-parameter ALM with a reward for agreement with clinicians improved claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while maintaining answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by dataset providers.

entry.title: Researchers propose Search-Native Pretraining to teach language models search capabilities during pretraining, improving knowledge-intensive task performance across model scales [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Search-Native Pretraining, a method that integrates web-search queries and retrieved responses into language model pretraining to teach models to generate search calls and use retrieved evidence. Experiments on Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora with models ranging from 360 million to 3.3 billion parameters show that search-pretrained models, called QueryLM, outperform or match larger baseline models on knowledge-intensive tasks and maintain advantages after supervised fine-tuning. The study suggests that conventional post-training does not fully capture search capabilities developed during pretraining, and the team has released training artifacts including model checkpoints and data.

entry.title: Researchers find label bias in LLM-as-judge evaluations is directional, inflating acceptance rates when few-shot examples skew positive [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied label bias in large language models (LLMs) used as judges to score open-ended outputs, focusing on a multimodal video question answering evaluation pipeline. They found that when the judge's few-shot examples were skewed toward acceptance, the acceptance rate increased sharply compared to human consensus, but skewing toward rejection did not produce a matching decrease, indicating a one-directional bias. The study also showed that results vary significantly depending on the specific examples drawn, suggesting that averaging over multiple draws and balancing examples can mitigate this bias. This directional label bias can artificially inflate benchmark scores but does not cause equivalent score drops, highlighting the importance of balanced prompting in LLM-based evaluation systems.

entry.title: Researchers present Baton, a method to transfer visual key-value memory from small to large vision-language models, reducing compute costs in video processing cascades [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Baton, a technique that allows a large vision-language model (VLM) to use the visual memory (key-value cache) generated by a smaller VLM, avoiding costly re-encoding of video history during escalations. Baton distills a per-layer linear map from the large model's responses, enabling efficient memory handoff without requiring a faithful cache copy. Experiments on RoboMME show Baton outperforms using the small model alone or re-watching frames, achieving similar accuracy with 28-47% less compute and eight times less cost per escalation at 64 frames. The method scales with larger models from 8 billion to 32 billion parameters and transfers zero-shot to other datasets like OpenEQA.

entry.title: ERA introduces a cold-start cross-model latent retrieval system using anchor-based adaptation and routing to reduce query latency and improve retrieval quality [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt) is a system designed to enable cold-start cross-model latent retrieval without re-embedding entire corpora when switching encoders. It selects informative anchor documents from an existing index, trains a lightweight adapter with manifold alignment loss to prevent representation collapse, and uses a deterministic router to escalate difficult queries that impact retrieval quality. Evaluated on five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms baseline methods, achieving up to 35% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on Arguana. It also reduces end-to-end query latency from about 160 ms to between 38 and 86 ms with minimal overhead, concentrating escalations on queries where the projection is less effective. This approach addresses the high cost and latency challenges of adapting retrieval systems to new embedding models at cold start.

entry.title: Researchers release PaMuk-Bench, a parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language models covering six languages and multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced PaMuk-Bench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) across multiple languages and tasks. It includes over 10,000 English prompts translated into Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, and Romanian, paired with generated and retrieved images to support tasks such as text-to-image generation, image captioning, and image retrieval difficulty estimation. The benchmark aims to address performance drops in low-resource languages due to limited annotated datasets. The benchmark's parallel translations were obtained through a semi-automatic process, enabling comparative development and evaluation of VLMs. Empirical results show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs perform worse than fine-tuned models, highlighting PaMuk-Bench's potential to reduce language gaps across various VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is publicly available for research use.

entry.title: Researchers propose statistical physics framework to model state transitions in LLM agents during post-training, demonstrating potential emergence in Qwen3.5-9B tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a statistical physics approach to analyze large language model (LLM) agents by defining agent states as intermediate variables to measure and predict post-training effects. They model state transitions using a global potential and a partition function representing an ideal KL-regularized transition distribution, tracking potential structure, mean reward, and state entropy. The approach is demonstrated on two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. Results show that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted, with correlated changes in reward and state entropy supporting the framework's consistency. This method provides a quantitative way to describe how post-training organizes agent behavior.

entry.title: Study compares decision models, large language models, and fine-tuned encoders for multilingual emotion classification across five languages and 10 social media datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated three decision models, two large language models (LLMs), and two fine-tuned multilingual encoders on classifying four emotions-joy, sadness, anger, and fear-in social media texts across five languages. The study found that the best zero-shot systems, including decision models and an LLM, performed close to fine-tuned encoders on target datasets, with an average macro-F1 score about one point lower, and outperformed encoders fine-tuned on different datasets by 8 to 15 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matched the performance of its underlying LLM at a fifth of the latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model outperformed a same-size general LLM by 10 points due to training rather than decision format.

entry.title: Researchers present OpinionGPT, a bias-aware instruction-tuned LLM fine-tuned on 11 demographic biases for transparent side-by-side comparison in a web demo [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed OpinionGPT, a web application that allows users to ask questions and receive answers reflecting explicit biases such as political, geographic, gender, and age perspectives. Instead of suppressing biases in instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), OpinionGPT makes them transparent by fine-tuning models on text written by members of distinct demographic groups. The underlying model was trained on an instruction-tuning corpus representing 11 different biases, enabling side-by-side comparison of responses based on selected biases. This approach aims to provide insight into how inherent biases affect LLM outputs rather than attempting to eliminate them.

entry.title: Researchers propose PS-GRPO to improve consistency in retrieval-augmented generation systems by training generators with group similarity rewards across paraphrased queries [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers address inconsistency in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, which often produce variable outputs for semantically equivalent queries, undermining reliability in high-stakes domains. They introduce an evaluation framework that breaks down consistency issues into retriever-level, generator-level, and end-to-end components to identify sources of inconsistency. To enhance consistency, they propose Paraphrased Set Group Relative Policy Optimization (PS-GRPO), a reinforcement learning method that uses group similarity rewards across paraphrased query sets to train generators to produce consistent outputs despite retrieval variability. The team applies PS-GRPO to develop Information Consistent RAG (Con-RAG), which improves output consistency while maintaining accuracy across various question-answering benchmarks without requiring explicit ground-truth supervision. They also introduce a scalable approximation to reduce computational costs of reward calculation, enabling efficient large-scale training. This work offers practical methods for evaluating and building more reliable RAG systems suitable for safety-critical applications.

entry.title: Researchers propose Agent-REINFORCE framework to optimize multi-LLM collaboration graphs for test-time scaling under fixed compute budgets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers address the challenge of optimizing test-time scaling (TTS) for large language models (LLMs) by searching for compute-optimal model combinations and architectures within fixed budgets. They formalize the problem as a multi-LLM collaboration graph with nodes representing roles and model assignments and edges capturing information flow, and propose Agent-REINFORCE, an LLM-agent-augmented framework that uses textual feedback as gradients to efficiently search for optimal collaboration graphs. The approach reformulates the combinatorial search as probabilistic graph optimization and leverages empirical insights from pilot experiments to guide the search process. Experiments demonstrate that Agent-REINFORCE outperforms traditional and LLM-based baselines in sample efficiency and search performance, effectively balancing accuracy and inference latency in multi-LLM collaboration designs.

entry.title: Researchers derive theoretical conditions where SignSGD outperforms SGD using ℓ1-norm lower bounds and demonstrate faster convergence in large model pretraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyze sign-based optimization algorithms like SignSGD and Muon, providing theoretical bounds under ℓ1-norm stationarity and ℓ∞-smoothness that identify problem classes where SignSGD reduces complexity by a factor of the problem dimension compared to SGD. They extend this framework to matrix domains for the Muon optimizer and validate their findings with experiments showing faster convergence during nanoGPT and LLaMA pretraining. This work bridges theoretical insights with practical performance improvements in training large foundation models.

entry.title: Researchers release CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that follows natural-language style prompts and achieves 1837 Elo without search
entry.summary: Researchers have developed CHSM8, a 210 million-parameter chess transformer that plays moves based on free-text descriptions of playing styles, such as "go for the Sicilian Defense" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime." The model was pretrained on 1.07 billion filtered Lichess games without search, using factorized move representation and legal-move masking, reaching 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and outperforming other public models trained without preference tuning or search. The team fine-tuned CHSM8 on a synthetic dataset with style descriptions, using supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization to improve style adherence while maintaining playing strength.

entry.title: Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.25760v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language-model agents often reason before they act, and the value of monitoring that reasoning depends on how it relates to their actions. We ask how an agent's actions depend on its reasoning when the correct action depends on a changing state. In a small file-system task, background events announce which file's lock has been toggled but not its new value. The agent therefore has to reconstruct the current locks from its history before it can move files safely. With Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B, we separate two roles of reasoning: generating it before each action, and retaining earlier reasoning in the prompt. Most of the reduction in lock-violating commands comes from reasoning written at the moment of action. Retaining earlier reasoning adds little when the agent also reasons at each step, but it helps an agent that does not reason, and it helps in longer episodes. Retained notes have a limit: when a later event makes a note wrong, an agent without current reasoning responds little, while current reasoning makes the action follow the event. The benefit depends on what the reasoning says. Filler text, reasoning written for another history and an accurate table of the state do not reproduce it. When we give the agent reasoning written for a history that differs in one lock value, the agent acts on that reasoning even against its own history. For Qwen3-8B, this holds also when that value has since been toggled. Without reasoning, state readouts are less reliable after toggles, and Qwen3-8B's answers about the state favor the outdated value. The state answer and the action also depend on different parts of the prompt. In this setting, the benefit of reasoning for rule-following comes mainly from generating it at each step, where it makes the action respond to later events. The state that can be read out without reasoning is a limited guide to how the agent acts.

entry.title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent study explored how the number and formation of AI agents in brainstorming teams affect human productivity and idea diversity. Conducted with 168 participants, the experiment compared teams with one versus two AI partners and varied AI behavior calibration. Findings showed that teams with two AI agents generated more ideas overall but saw a significant drop in human-authored contributions. When paired with a single AI calibrated to average human behavior, participants posted more ideas than in other setups. However, this effect disappeared with two AI partners, where humans engaged more in conversation but contributed fewer ideas to the shared board. Additionally, AI presence enhanced the overall diversity of human ideas, with two AI agents increasing differentiation within sessions. The study highlights that results from single-agent AI collaborations may not apply to multi-agent contexts, as team composition influences human participation and output.

entry.title: TOUMAII: A 4.5M-Pair Tool-Calling Preference Dataset and Its Source-Agnostic Generator [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To autonomously execute multi-step tasks, enterprise agents must reliably interact with tools, call APIs, or query databases, making tool-calling a fundamental capability of AI models. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) optimises for producing the correct call, but never contrasts it with a plausible incorrect one. In an environment where even a minor formatting error can invalidate a call and an incorrect decision can derail the interaction, direct preference optimisation (DPO) targets exactly this contrast. DPO, therefore, requires preference pairs rather than plain demonstrations. For tool-calling, such data, especially in realistic multi-turn settings, remains extremely scarce. To address this scarcity, we introduce TOUMAII, a large-scale tool-calling preference dataset containing ~4.5M validated preference pairs, derived from Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M (apache-2.0) conversations. The dataset consists of multi- and single-turn interactions and includes parallel and sequential function calls. Additionally, we release TOUMAII-Gen, a synthetic data generation pipeline that consumes tool-calling SFT datasets and generates a preference dataset with naturally occurring model-generated tool-calling failure modes. To validate the effectiveness of our DPO data, we fine-tune a 3-billion-parameter model, achieving performance parity with other high-quality tool-calling preference datasets. Furthermore, we release a second small preference dataset derived from ToolACE (apache-2.0), showcasing the source-agnostic nature of our pipeline. We release the complete code and datasets: https://github.com/tum-ai/toumaii-gen and https://huggingface.co/collections/tum-ai/toumaii-generated-datasets

entry.title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

entry.title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.

entry.title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.

entry.title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. Indeed, LLMs trained to predict the next token in text must exploit this predictive information, so its organization determines how the structure of language becomes available to the model to learn. We develop a theory for the organization of predictive information based on the scaling behavior of a family of information measures, and the theory predicts that if this organization has the same form at all measured length scales -- i.e., it has a self-similar structure -- then the information measures evaluated at different lengths collapse onto a common form. We observe this scaling collapse in long text documents, showing that predictive information is present at every length scale we measure and has a self-similar structure. Self-similarity is a considerably stronger property than showing the existence of long-range dependencies, and it constrains the process generating the text. More broadly, our results give quantitative support to the empirical observation that conditioning on more distant text continues to reveal new structure in language to LLMs.

entry.title: Right Numbers, Wrong Story: When LLMs Narrate Financial Changes Beyond Their Inputs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A financial report drafted by an LLM can state every number correctly but still go beyond its input, adding judgments and causes that no one supplied. We call these additions unsupported framing and find them far more often in LLM drafts than in reports written by proInput facts Revenue +3% Higher prices 10-K filings Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. 10-K writer Revenue surged 3% on higher prices, due to strong demand. LLM Fits the size? Surged: Unusual for 3% In the input? In the input? Strong demand: Not in input Higher prices: Kept fessionals, and attempts to fix them by prompting with how each word is used instead make such judgments more frequent. We therefore propose FrameCheck, a plug-in that sits beFrameCheck Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. No extra model call Judgment word Unsupported cause Supported cause tween the LLM and human review to keep each draft within its input. Specifically, FrameCheck 1) guides the draft with professional examples that report a change of similar magnitude, 2) flags judgments that professionals would not use and causes the input does not give, and 3) removes them by rule, without a model call. In experiments on 17 open LLMs and 3M drafts, FrameCheck removes almost all unsupported framing from drafts and brings the judgment rate close to that of the writers of 10-K filings, the annual reports that US firms file with regulators. Code is available at github.com/seunghan96/framecheck.

entry.title: From Letter-of-Credit Requirements to Executable Specifications: Evaluating Verification Accuracy and Completeness [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was examined. We therefore evaluate examination requirement by requirement and make each requirement executable. A language model converts the bill of lading (BL) and commercial invoice (IV) requirements of a credit into atomic conditions and logical structures, and a deterministic verifier retrieves the named evidence and computes each outcome, so every check can be compared with a gold encoding and traced to logged evidence. Because LC records are confidential, our on-premises 9B parser is fine-tuned only on synthetic pairs built from templates and human-reviewed public document values. On 345 real LC cases, final-decision accuracy proves misleading: a constant PASS rule has the highest raw accuracy while examining nothing. Although it never sees a real record during training, the fine-tuned parser detects 93% of the atomic requirements its ontology covers and reconstructs 86% of the covered requirements exactly. It verifies 82% of the evaluable requirements correctly, against 54% for a tool-using agent, and leads the agent on both satisfied requirements and discrepancies. It also completely examines 1.8 times as many cases as few-shot prompting of the same model, while direct prediction and the agent complete none. Executing the gold encodings with the same verifier shows that some of the remaining errors, missed discrepancies included, come from the operators and normalization, which a better parser alone cannot fix. Every rejection comes with a trace of the units and evidence behind it, which suits examiner-in-the-loop review.

entry.title: Integral Multipliers and Arithmetic Obstructions for Two-Hidden-Layer ReLU Maxima [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study exact representations of maximum functions by ReLU networks with two hidden layers and integer parameters. The least positive output multiplier is two for the six-input maximum, and either two or six for the seven-input maximum. We obtain these bounds from integral cubical fillings and a coefficient-preserving passage from polytope identities to networks. For the coordinate-facet complex of the six-simplex, we compute a coning index of six over the integers and three after inverting two, allowing arbitrary integral directions within each facet. A class in the homology of the unrestricted kernel complex characterizes the remaining seven-input problem; its vanishing is equivalent to an integral filling of a fixed target. We also construct a finite character that separates rational from three-local representability in a dictionary containing two known constructions and all pairs of edge-disjoint three-edge forests. This obstruction permits nonsymmetric coefficients and is confined to the specified dictionary. Control of lower-dimensional remainders yields a sufficient criterion in the top-dimensional quotient. Exact certificates and verification programs accompany the finite calculations.

entry.title: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.

entry.title: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.

entry.title: Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $\delta$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($\delta$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($\delta$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $\delta$ = 1 minus $\delta$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.

entry.title: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM simulations are validated by equivalence with human effects, yet a zero reference passes whenever the human 90 percent interval lies inside the margin, as the human benchmark shows before simulation. When the zero reference fails, planned precision gives independent simulations the margin up to which passing is a 5 percent test of response. In an exploratory 70-experiment reanalysis, 72 percent of GPT-4's $\pm$0.20 SD passes were zero-reference passes; GPT-4 passed 16 contrasts the zero reference failed (1.58 expected without response). In a preregistered audit, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed three intention targets, all zero-reference passes, and the registered belief-gradient control; norm beliefs changed 0.065 SD against humans' 0.351 (zero-reference check added after unblinding; norm beliefs emphasized after inspection). Registered tests detected no overestimation; average-effect intervals excluded overestimation above 0.08 SD. A group audit's precision floor is 1.33 facts against a 2.9-fact effect. Report the zero-reference threshold beside every equivalence decision.

entry.title: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current large language model (LLM) agents still struggle to forecast real-world events. This stems from two primary limitations: i) standard ReAct harness accumulates reasoning and evidence within one growing context, and ii) outcome-based rewards in forecasting lead to a slow and noisy signal that cannot distinguish sound reasoning from lucky guesses. To address these, we introduce a forecasting training framework including harness design and post-training. For the harness side, we propose Proactive Belief-State Management (PBM), equipping agents with a fold tool to compress lengthy context into compact belief states and reset the context for subsequent exploration. For the training side, we develop SEIPH, a five-dimensional, outcome-blind rubric, providing process-quality rewards. Using the rubric-based reward, we post-train a 35B model with PPO and GRPO, yielding DeepForecaster-PPO and DeepForecaster-GRPO. Theoretically, we prove that idealized fold-based stopping converges and calibrated local rewards reduce segment-level gradient variance. Empirically, DeepForecaster-PPO (35B) achieves the best Brier score on both ForecastBench and Polymarket-Sim, outperforming frontier agents based on DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T), Kimi-K2.6 (1T), and GPT-5.5. DeepForecaster-GRPO ranks second on both FutureX metrics. Ablations reveal that PBM also improves the untrained base model without any training. Calibration analysis shows that DeepForecaster-PPO makes more accurate high-confidence predictions than Qwen3.6 and GPT-5.5. Trajectory analysis further shows that forecasts generally improve from the first to the final belief state as agents gather evidence and revise their judgments.

entry.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

entry.title: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.

entry.title: Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Fault Detection and Structural Learning in Chemical Processes: Use Case on the Tennessee Eastman Process [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) methods, including many data-driven approaches, assume a static normal operating space and interpret deviations from a fixed reference as fault indicators. When Operating Conditions (OCs) vary over time, this assumption breaks down: legitimate transitions trigger false alarms while moderate faults go undetected. We propose a spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework that decomposes the normal operating space into OC-specific subspaces linked by transition functions, with a dual learning objective combining reconstruction loss and a Deep SVDD one-class term. It learns adjacency matrices through Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and integrates spatial modelling with temporal encoding to represent process dynamics under evolving OCs. This paper evaluates the framework's foundational components (fault detection, GATv2 spatial graph learning and temporal encoding) on the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark, training only on fault-free data. The architecture achieves competitive detection from reconstruction error alone, with similarity-based feature selection improving both accuracy and graph structure diversity. We then evaluate the physical interpretability of the learned attention matrices against 22 ground-truth sensor pairs derived from the TEP control structure and process topology. GATv2 attention fails to recover all known physical pairs across multiple hyperparameter configurations, suggesting a structural limitation of reconstruction-driven attention rather than a tuning issue. This challenges a common assumption in GNN-based FDD: that learned attention weights provide a basis for fault diagnosis and root-cause analysis. The architecture detects faults effectively, but the learned graph does not encode the physical topology needed for interpretable diagnosis, motivating physics-informed graph construction.

entry.title: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. To address this, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, a novel industrial architecture for automated UX attribution. Tier 1 (Macro System) acts as a scalable user sentiment regression detector, utilizing a fine-tuned encoder-decoder LLM (based on Gemini XS) on telemetry features. Through multi-task regularization and contextual feature engineering, this tier achieves a +9.8% PR-AUC gain on over 500,000 held-out records, matching baseline recall on all validated regressions with $\sim$20% relative precision gain among the 12 held-out experiments. In production, it reduces measurement latency from weeks to hours and cuts survey overhead by over 40%. Tier 2 (Micro System) provides granular diagnostics by employing a Multimodal LLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) to natively assess visual renderings and spatial layout of web result blocks, quantifying "User Toil" as the estimated effort required to reach a satisfactory result. Enhanced by RL-based automated prompt optimization and an AI judge for win/loss patterns, the MLLM yields a $>$6.5% F1 score improvement, offering deep insights into content quality and layout friction. Ultimately, this framework enables scalable, accurate, and diagnostic UX attribution, processing O(100k) live experiment queries daily.

entry.title: VerifiQuant: Governance-by-Execution for Financial LLM Workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26649v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models embedded in financial workflows fail most dangerously by emitting confident, well-formatted but wrong numbers with no signal distinguishing them from correct ones. We argue that the central deployment problem is governability: a system must determine when a question supports a numeric answer and when it should instead clarify, intercept, or refuse. We present VerifiQuant, a governance-by-execution framework that packages financial logic into inference contracts and evaluates each query through an executable diagnostic funnel before deterministic computation. This separation makes computation, clarification, and refusal structured and auditable while keeping financial arithmetic outside the language model. Against matched retrieval-and-execution baselines, and within a declared contract library, the principal benefit is not higher accuracy on well-posed questions but safer behavior when an input does not justify a number. When it finds no applicable contract, it says so instead of guessing. Coverage sweeps and failure analysis put a price on this boundary: safety is bought with coverage rather than with accuracy, and residual failures remain attributable to specific runtime frontiers.

entry.title: On the loss landscape of the linear neural network: beyond critical points [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While the critical points of the loss landscape in linear neural networks have been extensively studied since the seminal work of Baldi \& Hornik in the late 1980s, a description of this landscape at an intermediate or global scale is still lacking. Such a characterization is crucial, particularly as a substantial body of literature indicates that gradient descent circumvents critical points. The present article introduces an intermediate structure, termed the critical thalweg, which encompasses all critical points and exhibits key geometric properties. Beyond providing a geometric proof of Baldi \& Hornik's results using simpler assumptions than the existing literature, this framework offers a global view of the loss landscape that can be easily visualized in a two-dimensional plane. Empirical observations suggest that gradient descent is attracted toward the critical thalweg, along which the loss continues to decrease to its global minimum.

entry.title: Depth-Linked Residual Tokens for Multimodal Retrieval and Generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.

entry.title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.

entry.title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.

entry.title: Realistic Robustness Evaluation of Tabular Data Driven Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing adoption of Machine Learning (ML) models in high-stakes applications has raised critical concerns regarding their robustness against adversarial attacks. While extensive research has focused on adversarial example generation in image and text domains, the study of such examples in tabular data remains comparatively limited, despite its widespread use in real-world systems. This work introduces AURORA, a modular, open-source tool for evaluating the robustness of ML models on tabular data classification. It integrates multiple adversarial perturbation methods and evaluation metrics within a unified framework to systematically assess model behavior under adversarial conditions. Central to AURORA is its evaluation report, which focuses on robustness analysis by quantifying performance degradation, comparing the impact of different perturbation strategies, and identifying model vulnerabilities across features and input regions. The report is complemented by visual artifacts that facilitate the interpretability of robustness patterns. Additionally, AURORA incorporates a distance adjustment mechanism that penalizes implausible adversarial samples based on feature-level constraints, ensuring that the robustness assessment remains grounded in realistic perturbations and is therefore more reliable.

entry.title: Rethinking Full-Weight LoRA with Domain and Task Adapter Scaling for Question Answering over Portuguese Well Drilling Reports [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains remains challenging, particularly for technical documents such as Portuguese well drilling reports, where annotated data are scarce and domain adaptation may compromise instruction-following capabilities. Although Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is widely used for parameter-efficient adaptation, its scaling after training remains insufficiently explored. This study investigates the impact of LoRA adapter scaling on question answering over Portuguese drilling reports using Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. Domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT) is performed either directly on instruction-tuned models or on their base counterparts, with subsequent adapter transfer, while task-specific adapters are trained on WellQuest, an open-source question-answering dataset derived from Portuguese drilling reports. The two adapters are also combined using complementary weights. Scaling factors ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 are evaluated across multiple training checkpoints using BERTScore. Results show that fractional scaling consistently improves DAPT performance over full-weight application, increasing F1 from 68.8\% to 71.9\% for Qwen2.5-7B and from 63.2\% to 68.5\% for Llama-3.1-8B. QA adapters perform best at high but fractional weights, while base-to-instruct transfer yields better results than direct DAPT on instruct-tuned models. Adapter merging provides a modest improvement for Llama-3.1-8B. Overall, these findings demonstrate that post-training adapter scaling can improve domain adaptation without additional data or training.

entry.title: Non-Expanding Gated Continued Fraction Architecture for Feedforward Layers in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets

entry.title: Scoliosis5K: Multimodal Gait Analysis via Clip-Conditioned RGB-Silhouette Fusion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Color walking video records body boundary motion alongside clothing folds, surface appearance, and recording-environment cues. To examine what an explicit binary silhouette contributes to participant-level classification of scoliosis-related gait when a classifier already observes the paired color sequence, we construct Scoliosis5K, a multi-site collection of 4,998 corridor-walking sequences across 3,010 participant identifiers in which RGB person crops, binary silhouettes, and two-dimensional poses share each recording identifier and frame index. Our architecture uses each patch's pixel deviation from its clip mean to weight two low-rank query and value updates inside a pretrained RGB encoder, fusing the resulting video representation with a silhouette transformer sequence and regional kernel ridge scores extracted from one native-resolution RGB frame per window. Across 988 participants in five participant-disjoint cross-validation folds and three training seeds, the complete system reaches 83.77% accuracy and 79.91% macro-averaged F1, compared with 83.27% accuracy and 79.56% macro-F1 when the video RGB encoder remains frozen under identical inputs. Zeroing the silhouette vector at fixed weights shifts overall accuracy by only 0.10 percentage points while raising positive-category recall from 68.52% to 77.78% and lowering recall for both remaining categories. Macro-averaged AUROC is 0.950 across the cohort and 0.879 among participant pairs matched on acquisition site and recording-count group.

entry.title: LoCo-WAM: Test-Time Training as Long Context for World-Action Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26853v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.

entry.title: ProbeAgent: Principled Diagnosis of Agent Failures in Verifiable Environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving agents requires discovering where they fail and understanding why. An agent acts over multiple steps in a changing environment, so diagnosing its failures requires more than inspecting the final response of a large language model (LLM). The same unsuccessful outcome can arise from task difficulty or from an error the agent repeats across tasks. We introduce ProbeAgent, an automated framework that discovers agent failures, tests their proposed causes, and identifies shared failure modes. Starting from benchmark tasks, ProbeAgent builds executable tests and validates them using reference solutions, automated checks, and review of the task requirements. For each failed trajectory, it explains the error and constructs new tasks that preserve the suspected cause while changing the surrounding context. Running the agent on these tasks tests whether the same error recurs. ProbeAgent then groups failures with similar causes and generates descriptions that distinguish their errors. This process connects explanations of individual failures to executable tests and descriptions of shared failure modes. We evaluate ProbeAgent across 22 agent configurations using tasks from 10 benchmarks, collecting 1,244 failures and producing 536 failure-mode descriptions. These descriptions distinguish specific errors within broad outcomes such as incomplete work, including planning without acting and stopping before delivering a file. In human evaluation, annotators accept 90.0% of assigned descriptions and correctly reject 83.3% of similar alternatives, supporting the accuracy and specificity of the discovered failure modes.

entry.title: Modeling Attributional Style at Scale: A Dataset and Analysis for Psychological Attribution Assessment and Reframing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: According to the reformulated Learned Helplessness theory, repeated exposure to uncontrollable negative events can foster a depressogenic attributional style, increasing susceptibility to depression yet remaining a tractable target for cognitive therapy. Computational research on attributional cognition, however, is hampered by the lack of large-scale datasets and robust evaluation protocols. In this work, we introduce the Attributional Style Transfer Dataset (ASTD) along with dedicated evaluation metrics, the first benchmark designed to model, assess, and reframe attributional explanations at scale. Constructed via a Prevent-Filter-Validate pipeline that integrates LLM-based generation with specialist validation, ASTD contains 42,000 real-world events paired with psychologically grounded attributions spanning seven styles. Using this dataset, we address two key challenges: (1) scalable assessment of attributional style via both supervised classifiers and zero/few-shot LLMs; and (2) attributional reframing and evaluation, where we propose automatic evaluation metrics to quantify psychological validity. Furthermore, we leverage our proposed metrics to construct a preference dataset, fine-tuning LLMs with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and achieving substantial gains in reframing quality. Together, our dataset, metrics, and methodology offer a new paradigm for understanding and modeling attributional style, with direct implications for scalable and adaptive mental health interventions. Code and data: https://github.com/qzhou711/ASTD

entry.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.

entry.title: SecretAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Privacy Protection against Vision Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26936v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.

entry.title: CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.

entry.title: Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.

entry.title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.26999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. Second, the language decision model (e.g., \jev{}) reads these indicators together with the customer's profile and activity, judges the case in context with broad world knowledge, and returns the score of high risk. We evaluate JevRisk on the anti-money laundering task with public synthetic data from Scotiabank and on the credit risk task with real data from Home Credit and Lending Club. On both tasks, JevRisk outperforms rule-based and unsupervised methods, and is on par with or better than supervised methods (e.g., GBDT and TabPFN) trained on about a thousand labelled customers.

entry.title: Ruby: State-of-the-Art Potency Prediction across Discovery Regimes Using Learned Structural Representations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.27015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small-molecule drug discovery proceeds through repeated design-make-test-analyze cycles. The goal is often to maximize potency while keeping other properties within the ranges required for a viable therapeutic candidate.
